speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Acting Prime Minister and ask who was responsible for the muddle which prevented Canada from being represented by a cabinet minister at the funeral of Prime Minister Nehru.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SAINT JOHN, N.B.-TRANSFER OF MANUFACTUR- ING FIRM TO MONTREAL
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CANADIAN MINISTERIAL REPRESENTATION AT NEHRU FUNERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been no muddle in respect of Canadian representation at the funeral ceremony of the late prime minister of India. The government had hoped and had endeavoured to see to it that a member of the government would attend the funeral. Because of the generous invitation of the President of the United States and the U.S. secretary of state, a Canadian representative was offered an opportunity to fly to India in the presidential plane.

Unfortunately, because of the time of the funeral it was not possible for the presidential plane in Washington to wait until the arrival from Ottawa of a minister. The Minister of National Defence had made preparations; he had gone to the airport in Ottawa; but we were advised that in order to enable the representative of the government of the United States to be in India in time for the funeral, the plane would have to leave Washington ahead of the scheduled hour of departure.
Canada was represented at the funeral this morning by the ambassador of Canada in Cairo, Mr. Jean Chapdelaine, our high commissioner in Ceylon and the charge d'affaires of our mission in Delhi.

Mr. Speaker, I have now received a full report concerning the case of Mr. Harry Hooper and have discussed it with my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I find that Hooper was in custody during the period of February 25, 1964 until Tuesday of this week, but this incarceration was not by any means related only to the charge which was preferred against him under section 50(e) of the Immigration Act.
He was first taken into custody by the metropolitan Toronto police on a charge of having assaulted his estranged wife. This charge was subsequently withdrawn on March 15. This part of the detention was therefore under provincial authority.
He continued in detention under the authority of the Immigration Act as a person believed to be in Canada unlawfully and subject to deportation. He had been deported on three previous occasions. The first time was in March 1962, and this order was based on the fact that Hooper had been convicted at Toronto on January 4, 1961, for having been in possession of a drug in violation of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.
The Immigration Act provides that persons who are deported shall not return without specific permission from the minister, but notwithstanding this Hooper returned to Canada without authority and was deported a second time on February 26, 1963. He again entered Canada illegally and was deported a third time on January 4, 1964. He returned three days later.
The inquiry with respect to his fourth unlawful entry got under way on March 23, after he had been given ample opportunity to retain counsel if he wished to do so. At the inquiry he refused to answer questions put to him by the special inquiry officer. The Immigration Act provides that such refusal is an offence punishable on summary conviction. Because of Hooper's refusal the special inquiry officer found it necessary to adjourn the hearing to April 7, at which time other evidence was adduced to establish his unlawful entry and he was ordered deported to the United States, of which country he is a citizen. He did not appeal against the order.
The next step in the sequence of events was this. Immigration officials at Toronto decided to refer the case to immigration headquarters

Inquiries of the Ministry in Ottawa for instructions on whether to execute the deportation order immediately or take steps to have a charge preferred in relation to Hooper's refusal to answer questions put to him at the inquiry. In this connection it should be noted that the Immigration Act provides that a person who commits an offence under the act is liable to be prosecuted and to undergo punishment notwithstanding that a deportation order has been made against him.
It was decided to prefer the charge, but in the making and implementing of this decision there was a lengthy delay and the charge was not laid until May 22. Hooper was brought before a magistrate on that date and the case was adjourned until May 25. Because of the delay between the making of the deportation order and the preferring of the charge it was decided it should be withdrawn, and this was done with the permission of Magistrate Bigelow on Tuesday of this week.
Certain delays were occasioned in the administrative machinery in processing this matter, but I can assure hon. members that steps have been taken, after discussion between myself and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, to prevent the repetition of such an occurrence in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the four minutes I had yesterday afternoon before five o'clock I made a few introductory remarks, and for the sake of continuity I will refer briefly to the comments I made yesterday.
I said that this bill, No. S-17, was gutless, was a hoax and a gross deception; that it was designed for two purposes, one, to make it appear that the promise of the Liberal party and of the Prime Minister is being met and, second, to make it appear that the 12 mile fishing limit is being established by way of this bill.
I have here a valuable document. It is a page from the Victoria Daily Colonist of March 31, 1963. It is headed "The Policies of the Liberal Party". It is a full page advertisement, and as I say it is a valuable document and one which gets more valuable by the day as we approach another election. This document is a clear indictment of the Liberal party, containing as it does a record of the promises which have been made and which have not been fulfilled.
This attempt to make it appear that the promise regarding the 12 mile limit is being fulfilled is, I say, a hoax. Included in the promises set out in this advertisement is a commitment to establish a 12 mile limit for offshore fishing. I notice that the hon. member for Victoria is in his place. I remember so well how in the last two elections he and his friends accused the previous government of doing nothing about the establishment of a 12 mile fishing limit. The facts are, of course, that our government in the United Nations conventions of 1958 and 1960 tried to get United Nations approval for our formula of six miles and six miles. Indeed, it came within one vote of having this formula approved in 1960. In subsequent years our government continued its efforts to negotiate agreements with the other governments involved.
The Liberals, of course, said they could get this accomplished on a unilateral basis; they were the only ones who could do it. This promise, Mr. Speaker, falls into the same category as many of the others which appear in this advertisement. I might mention, for example, the reform of taxes. Well, they reformed them; they increased them. Then there are the promises concerning student loans,

speechtext:
The minister says there is a base line now based on sinuosities. That is true. But the 12 mile limit based on a fixed line will not be in effect until the co-ordinates are named by order in council.
Both the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries have stated that the passage of this bill would assist the government in negotiating with the other countries involved on such matters as historic rights, traditional rights and treaty rights. My question is immediate; if this bill is to be valuable in this respect now, would it not have been even more valuable when negotiations were begun many months ago? Further, if this bill places the government in a better position to negotiate, would not the government be in a much stronger position now if it could tell us at least the co-ordinates for the major bodies of water in which commercial fishermen and others are interested? On the west coast, for instance, there is Hecate strait, Queen Charlotte sound, the Dixon entrance, and so on.
The secretary of state, giving evidence before members of the other place, said he hoped negotiations with the other countries concerned would be ended in the latter part of the year. If that is so, why could not the present bill have been delayed until these important matters could have been referred to in it? In that case we would be given something concrete to consider.
The minister has indicated that the bill will be sent to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. However, nothing at all appears in the measure now before us with

regard to a number of important matters with which the people in this business are concerned. I have in mind the co-ordinates on which the base line will be measured, the question of which waters will be considered Canadian waters, the question of the extent to which historic and traditional rights will be recognized, and so on. There is nothing in the bill before us about which the committee could ask questions or hear evidence. The minister might tell the committee what it is intended to do or what it is hoped to do, but there is no meat in this proposal for a committee to get its teeth into.
The minister has agreed that the bill will not come into force until it is proclaimed, and that the base line will have no meaning until the co-ordinates are made known. Why rush this measure through now, when there is so much important legislation on the order paper and when so many other major matters are still to be put down for parliamentary consideration? We are spending our time considering a bill which means nothing whatever.
We shall be able to go into greater detail at a later stage, but with regard to part II I have a letter sent to me by MacLaren, Laid-law and Corlett, solicitors in this city acting on behalf of nine international air lines. I quote from a brief or memorandum they submitted respecting this bill. These agents of these nine international air lines are concerned with regard to part II of the bill. As the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) said, according to the bill it is possible for instance, for the government by order in council to name some point on Sable island as one of the co-ordinates to establish a base line. We accept the assurance of the minister that they will not do that, but this is what the representatives of these nine international air lines say:
The present government might quite properly deny that they had any intention of using Sable island as a geographical co-ordinate. However, our point is that as section 5(1) of Bill S-17 is presently worded any future government could make such a choice by order in council without having to come back to parliament for amending legislation.
Mr. Speaker, there is concern in their minds because it is possible for some future government to establish co-ordinates, in order to make concessions to other countries, for which they would not have to account directly to the house. I would appeal to the government If they will not agree to having this bill sent to committee before second reading so the committee could go into the whole matter of the principle involved, then at least at the committee stage the government should attach to the bill a schedule indicating the co-ordinates to be used to measure the base

lines for the important bodies of water. This is the point about which the people in the business are concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to reply to some of the criticism of this bill which has been voiced from the opposition benches. At this stage on second reading we are concerned mainly with the principle of the bill, and the principle is certainly very clear. It is, do we want a 12 mile territorial limit or do we not? It is very simple; you are either for it or you are against it.
Most of the speeches from the opposition benches have criticized the details of the bill, which criticism would be more appropriate at the committee stage. As the minister has already said that it will be examined by the standing committee on marine and fisheries, surely that will provide every opportunity to bring out all the various points with regard to the details of the bill in which hon. members opposite are interested.
The criticism that has been voiced so far mainly concerns four points. The first point is that this bill is of no consequence; that it is a hoax, a deception and a pretence of keeping an election promise. That point was taken mainly by the hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich, who has just resumed his seat. The second criticism is that it should not have been introduced until all the multilateral agreements had been secured. The third criticism has been that this bill gives recognition to treaty and historic rights.
All this criticism, with the exception of that offered by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), who replied to the minister on behalf of the Conservative party and who I believe was very fair in his comments, to date has been rather negative and there has been nothing constructive or positive. The kindest thing that I think can be said about it is that it has been based on a lack of understanding of the bill. Certainly that was very clear in the remarks of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, because my understanding of the bill is quite different from his in the way he outlined it to the house.
Most legislation falls into two classes. One class is called declaratory; it brings something into existence. The second class is known as enabling legislation because it authorizes the government to do something or try to do something. This particular bill is both because when it is proclaimed, or at least when a certain section of it is proclaimed, it will create a nine mile fishing zone adjacent to our present territorial waters. In the face of that fact, how can any intelligent person say that this bill is a hoax or is of no consequence? Our present three
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones mile territorial waters, with the exception of the Newfoundland coast line waters, are based on what is called the sinuosity principle, which means that they are measured straight off from the shore and consequently follow the indentations and contours of the coast line.
If hon. members are interested in knowing why Newfoundland is a little different in this respect, I can tell them that it is based on an interpretation by The Hague tribunal of a treaty between the United States and Great Britain. The treaty dates back to 1818 but the interpretation of The Hague tribunal was made in 1910 and established the headland to headland principle. Newfoundland, as an autonomous, self governing part of the British empire, adopted this headland to headland principle in defining its territorial sea and brought that principle with her when she became part of Canada.
To the extent that the section of this bill, when proclaimed, will establish unilaterally a fishing zone extending 12 miles off from headland to headland along the Newfoundland coast line, and 12 miles from land along the remainder of the Canadian coast line, the bill is declaratory. If nothing else happens, we will have established jurisdiction over the conservation and harvesting of our fishery resources in a belt of water extending 12 miles from land, and that is certainly a big improvement over what we now have.
But this particular bill goes further than that. It will give the government enabling powers, authorized by parliament, to do two things more. First, as I understand it, it will enable the government to delineate a new zone of territorial waters, based not on the sinuosity principle as at present but on the base line principle, which I believe is a variation of the headland to headland principle extended to include offshore islands. In the second place it will give the government enabling powers to delineate a new fishing zone adjacent to and extending seaward nine miles outside the new territorial waters. In other words the jurisdiction over the conservation and harvesting of our fishery resources will be measured 12 miles seaward from the base line instead of 12 miles from land as at present. This will enclose a much larger area of water and will also create new inland waters which will greatly facilitate conservation measures, particularly with regard to our seal fishery. It will also have significance from the standpoint of national security.
In establishing any delineation of territorial waters realistic people must realize that there must be exceptions to the general rule. Obviously the general rule of a 12 mile limit cannot be applied where there is less than

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones 12 miles of water between the coast line of Canada and that of a foreign country. A very good example of that lies near my own constituency. I refer to the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, which at their nearest point are only nine miles distant from the coast line of the Burin peninsula in my riding, the average distance between the two coast lines being somewhere around 15 miles. Obviously neither country can have a 12 mile territorial limit under those conditions, so that the sensible thing to do is to work out a mutually satisfactory arrangement.
The same applies to historic rights, which in the case of some nations are embodied in treaties and have become treaty rights. If I understand the position taken by the hon. member for New Westminster, which was described in the editorial which he placed on record yesterday and which he obviously endorses, he would have us tear up these treaties and brush them aside like scraps of paper. I do not think any member of parliament would seriously want Canada to behave in such a manner. In any case it is not very responsible behaviour, and is certainly not a good position from which to start bargaining.
I do not know what is the situation on the Pacific coast, but I can tell hon. members what the position is in my own riding. Certain European countries have fished in the coastal waters of Newfoundland, particularly those of my own riding, for over 400 years. They have fished there continuously. The French islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon again afford a good example. The economy of both these islands depends largely on the inshore fishery. The French fishermen use the same inshore fishing grounds as the Newfoundland fishermen whom I have the honour to represent. They experience the same hardships and vicissitudes of life and make about the same kind of living, just enough to keep body and soul together but not much more. I would not want to deprive those St. Pierre fishermen of their historic and treaty rights upon which their livelihood depends. I would not want to take their bread and butter out of their mouths and the mouths of their children, any more than I want French, Spanish and Portuguese draggers to deprive my own fishermen, particularly in the Rose Blanche area, of their livelihood. We want to live and let live. We want to do what is right by them as we expect them to do what is right by us. If these St. Pierre fishermen did not have any rights I would certainly want them to have rights, because they are people. Their livelihood depends upon those rights, and people are certainly more important than politics.
The position which this bill takes is that treaty rights and historic rights do exist. The honest thing to do is to recognize this fact 

and get together and work out the best course to take. Let us decide what is the right thing to do in the light of all the circumstances for all concerned, and which at the same time will take care of the problems which are troubling us.
The fourth criticism has been that this bill should not have been introduced until multilateral agreements had been secured. Exploratory talks have been going on in connection with this matter for the past ten years. It was recognized ten years ago that the present three mile territorial limit was not suited to Canada's needs. Unless we show that we mean business by passing this legislation, these talks could very well go on for another ten years with still nothing accomplished. That would be an even worse deception than what hon. members opposite say about this bill, because we would have to keep talking and talking indefinitely without any clear achievement or sign of achievement.
If we really mean business in this matter, as I am sure we do, it seems to me that the proper thing to do is to pass the legislation which shows that we mean business, and then start the formal talks which are necessary to work out the problems connected with the establishment of the base lines from which our new territorial waters and the new fishing zone will be measured.
Canada has a good reputation among our neighbours for the way in which she has honoured and respected her treaties, and for her relationships with other countries. We want to maintain that reputation. In this regard I should like to put on record a paragraph from an editorial in yesterday's issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, which reads as follows:
In international law Canada has a good but not incontestable case for its actions. If a contest arose, they might or might not be upheld by the international court. Perhaps the countries affected will agree to Canada's moves, perhaps they will not; and perhaps we cannot afford to ignore their objections.
All of this, of course, remains to be seen. In the meantime the government deserves to be commended for its determination to press this vital issue forward.
Parliament should grant the government the authority it requests.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as for my own province and my own constituents, we have waited long and patiently for this legislation. We are happy that it is at last before this house. It has tremendous significance not only for the future of the fishing industry but for the security of our country. It has a special significance for my own province, where the fishing industry has played a dominant role in our economy for over 400 years.

It is even more significant for the people of my own riding, especially those engaged in the inshore fishery around the Rose Blanche and Port aux Basques area who year after year have had their gear destroyed and have been denied the fishing grounds by foreign draggers at the very time when the fishery is at its peak, thus having to remain ashore and watch themselves and their families being deprived of their livelihood. We welcome this legislation and I support this bill without any reservation whatsoever.
I want to close with one final word to the government. I wish to emphasize the need of urgency in this matter. Time is of the essence. Already too many long years have passed without action in this regard. Without detracting from anything that was done by the former government-and I am prepared to give that government full credit for the efforts they made in this regard and to say we are benefiting from what they did-the time has now come to carry this matter one stage further and not to waste time debating the principle, because this legislation is very urgently needed and the sooner it can be passed the better for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, may I start by making a brief reference to the closing remarks of my good friend from Burin-Burgeo. I say to him that debating this measure is not a waste of time. Precisely because of its importance it is most necessary to debate it to ensure in every possible way that the fisheries of our nation and the rights and opportunities of our fishermen are protected. That being so, in my opinion any suggestion that debating this bill is a waste of time is spurious and facetious, and the house should not be asked to approach the matter in that manner.
It is perhaps appropriate that at this time in our history we are now concerned, or will be concerned within the next few days, with two matters relating to our sovereignty. The bill before us is one of them. It involves the sovereignty and authority of the government of Canada in an area where they did not exist before but should have existed. The other matter concerns the attitude of sovereignty and independence which apparently has found its way into the heart of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and is exemplified in the design for a flag which he put before us the other day.
There is a similarity between these two matters. We are asked to think of the proposed flag as being symptomatic of our sovereignty, our national identity and the unity which exists within Canada. With respect to this bill we are being asked to make an
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones initial declaration to be followed by certain orders in council which again will involve our sovereignty, national identity and unity.
The bill before us involves resources of our nation, namely, those of the sea. It involves the application of sovereignty in relation to the conservation and protection of our fisheries resources. To my mind these two measures seem to go hand in hand. I cannot say whether it was by accident or design that the government saw fit to introduce them at this particular time. This is something that the government alone knows. But if it was by design, if the government planned to introduce into the forum of parliament and into the minds of the Canadian people the flag on the one hand and the proposal for a 12 mile fishing zone on the other, I think the government deserves to be congratulated to some extent because of the opportunity that is afforded to us to make a thorough inquiry into all aspects of the two measures, as those aspects are related to each other, because they involve our sovereignty and because they involve what many of us have been striving for for many years, namely, an autonomous Canada which manages its own affairs and does not have to bow to the desires or interests of other nations.
In the proposal for a flag we really have not a two flag policy but one might say more appropriately a two faced policy, involving the union jack and the so-called distinctive Canadian flag of which the Prime Minister at least is enamoured. If that is the approach to be taken it is also pleasant to realize that among the people of the province of Quebec there is a great desire for compromise on this matter, and that if the flag resolution on the order paper is accepted it will mean that in the province of Quebec there will be acceptance of the union jack as emblematic of something which is perhaps dearer to some people in Canada than to others.
I also submit that the bill before us is a two faced proposal like the flag and represents the attitude of a government that tries to do everything both ways, that tries to sell the Canadian people a bill of goods on the one hand and tries to protect the interests of others on the other hand, a government that tells us it is doing something for our protection while at the same time it is really catering to the whims and desires of some other part of the world. The purpose of the bill before us has been described in press releases and elsewhere as being to put into effect an exclusive fishing zone. This is part of the two faced policy because it will not be an exclusive fishing zone if the bill becomes law. There will in fact be the maintenance of the privilege which France and the United States have had for

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones 150 to 200 years to fish within the proposed 12 mile zone and to continue to do so, not for 10 years or 20 years or some period at the end of which this would cease but forever. Forever is a blessed long time for these rights to fish in our waters to be continued. In this sense the policy is a two faced one.
On the one hand we are asked to adopt a distinctive flag emblematic of our feeling of independence and unity and on the other hand we are doing every blessed thing we can to preserve the conditions in treaties made with foreign powers without doing anything to try to negotiate any change in the terms of those treaties. It is claimed that the bill reflects a decision on the part of the government to take unilateral action, but again this is an indication of a two faced approach because the bill does not provide for such unilateral action at all.
One of the prime bases upon which the bill rests is the basis of negotiation with all the other countries that have or claim treaty or historic fishing rights in the area which we propose to embrace within the 12 mile fishing zone. I will not bother to read the quotation from Hansard, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has referred at different times to negotiations that are taking place. This, again, is an indication of a two faced approach. We claim this is a unilateral decision on the one hand, and on the other hand we say it is not because we are negotiating with these other countries. The Secretary of State for External Affairs shakes his head. His words are in Hansard. His words are there for posterity to see and for anybody to read. His words are in the reports of the proceedings of the Senate banking and commerce committee before which he appeared as a witness. He may shake his head, but the shaking of his head will not act as an eraser and rub out those words, no matter how rubbery the situation might be. These words will remain.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) have said they are negotiating with other countries. They spelled out these various negotiations.

I do not know which coat the minister is wearing at the moment, but


in so far as this bill is concerned I shall refer to him as the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would just say that he has just proven he is the best actor we have ever had in this house, whether as prime minister or in any other position. His words will not cover up the fact that we are negotiating with the other countries in respect of this particular bill. He shakes his head again. As I have said, no matter how many times he shakes it, it will not act like the eraser on the end of a pencil. His words will remain in Hansard for all to see.
It is claimed on the one hand that this bill is designed to protect our fisheries. At the same time, both the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries have said that never at any time was it our intention to interfere in any way, to abrogate or even change the treaties which are in existence which give specific rights to foreign countries to fish within this area. Never at any time was it their intention to do this. On the one hand they refer to protection to the fullest extent, but this protection applies to nations other than the United States and France. They talk about conservation in the same way. This is designed to conserve our fisheries, while at the same time they want to allow foreign nations to fish in these areas.
We have with respect to the flag a proposal for some national identity which I submit is a design or proposal developed primarily to suit one province. With regard to the 12 mile fishing zone proposal before us, it is designed primarily to suit one nation. In so far as the flag matter is concerned, may I just quote briefly from a letter which I received a few days ago and which reads as follows:
The plan for a distinctively national flag for Canada, under the present method of Mr. Pearson's is just another sop to Quebec. While no doubt he feels it politically expedient to defer to Quebec in most matters, it is getting to be too much. Why should a minority of five million, because of threats or other forms of blackmail, make 14 to 15 million others bow to their wishes?

My friend asks if I would go for it. This is not worthy of an answer. I do not want to be drawn into these snide comments by the member who continues his speech while in a sitting position. If occasionally he would like to rise formally I would be glad to debate matters with him.
We have before us a particular motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) that the subject matter of this bill be referred to a standing committee. The argument has been made outside of this house, more than in it, that if the motion carries the government would be defeated and there would be an election. Why that was said, I do not know, unless it constitutes a threat of some sort.
My position with regard to voting on want of confidence motions that may be moved in respect of this government is well known. However, this in no way interferes with my feelings or attitude on a measure such as this. If in the process of voting on the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, it happens to carry and the government is defeated, that is well and good. We will at least have something concrete and worth while to talk about during the election campaign. The argument used that this would cause the defeat of the government is not really well founded, unless the government wants it that way.
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones
Perhaps I could make reference to an action which took place last year in which there were two bills before the house dealing with an attempt to divide the Northwest Territories into two territories, one of which would be the new territory of Nunassiaq. It was after some extended discussion on those bills that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who then had the position of house leader, on November 15, 1963 moved a motion which received the endorsation of everyone in the house, because parliament was desirous to take that course of action, a motion that the subject matter of the two bills be referred to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters for consideration. Then there was the important proviso:
-provided however, that despite this motion the said bills shall remain on the order paper as orders for second reading without prejudice to the right to make or proceed with motions for such second reading.
This is what we suggest should take place here in an equally important matter, in a matter equally important as was the proposal to split the territories into two, or perhaps more important because the livelihood, welfare and rights of more people are involved. We suggest this is the course of action the government should take, and that it should acquiesce in the request to refer the subject matter of the bill to the marine and fisheries committee, and keep the bill on the order paper so that we can come back to it.
I suggest this for the very simple reason that a course of that kind will allow the committee to examine this question in its broadest possible aspects because, when we are taking steps to declare a 12 mile limit, or any other mile fishing limit, we must take into account that various species of fish, notably salmon, do not know where that 12 mile limit is, and might occasionally swim outside it and get caught by fishermen of other nations.
This is of vital importance, particularly to the west coast. We should give the committee an opportunity to go extensively into the north Pacific fisheries commission operations and to make as extensive examination as possible into the detrimental effect that high seas fisheries in the mid-Pacific might have on the salmon stocks of B.C., because the salmon stocks are declining year after year, and because year after year fishermen from Japan are increasing their catch of salmon by leaps and bounds. Japan does not contribute materially, or what it does contribute is insignificant to the salmon stocks which intermingle in the mid-Pacific and north Pacific area.

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones
The committee should be asked to inquire extensively into that to determine the degree, if any, by which the proposed 12 mile limit will be beneficial to the stocks here at home. I submit that it won't matter one whit but, if the committee is able to make an examination of that sort, it will be able to look at the possibilities and make recommendations about the content of the expected new treaty between the United States, Japan and Canada, and might be able to make some worthwhile recommendations to bring into effect the Liberal pledge of a few years ago to draw the Soviet union into the north Pacific fisheries treaty.
We should also examine into the fact that the Soviet union and Japan recently amended a treaty which they have between themselves regarding Japanese high seas fisheries on the Asian side of the Pacific, with one of the provisions being that two thirds of the catch that Japan makes of salmon on the high seas must come from the area bounded by the 175th west meridian, which is the line of demarcation in the Pacific over which Japan, up until now, has agreed not to fish.
What will happen as a result of this agreement between Russia and Japan is that the Japanese high seas fishing fleet will be moving closer and closer to the mid-Pacific fisheries and creating greater and greater pressures upon the stocks of salmon that intermingle in that area, and also upon the stocks of salmon from Alaska. The committee should inquire into the full implications of that, so that we can look at the fisheries question as it is, as a whole, and not at one little section, namely the extension of the fishing zones.
We also have the situation in northern B.C. where United States fishermen on the northern side of the Alaska boundary just sit and wait there for our sockeye and pink salmon to come home to spawn, and scoop up our home-coming salmon to suit themselves, without any of our fishery regulations having an effect on them. Partially as a result we find the fishermen on the Skeena river being confined to fishing for sockeye on the basis of about one day a week during the present season.
We want the committee to inquire extensively into that and see if it can make recommendations about treaties, or arrangements between the two countries so that our home-coming salmon, that do escape the high seas fisheries, are not caught by United States fishermen when they are nearing the spawning grounds.
Also in the north we have the extremely important question that some of the spawning rivers are in Canadian territory but their

mouths are in Alaskan territory. One such river is the Stikine. This is a matter which should be a subject of discussion between the two nations, and it is a matter which the 12 mile limit cannot remedy.
On the Atlantic coast we have the ridiculous situation where some of our fishing vessels have to go outside 12 miles to fish, yet we allow foreign fishing vessels to come in and disturb whatever conservation measures we put into effect.
For these reasons we ask the government to accept the proposal that we refer the subject matter to the marine and fisheries committee, and leave the bill on the order paper so that it may be dealt with at any time. Let us give to the committee the broadest possible scope of inquiry so that it may come up with recommendations that would be helpful and beneficial to our fishermen and helpful to the preservation of the fisheries of this nation.

All we would be doing would be to endorse the principles, or lack of them, contained in this bill and then give to a cabinet, which is weak and divided on this as it is on most other issues, endorsa-tion to negotiate as it wishes.
In the conduct of negotiations, if I were a member of a union and the Secretary of State for External Affairs were my business agent *-a highly unlikely situation if I had any part in it-I would not want him to negotiate on my behalf in the way he is seeking to negotiate on behalf of Canada and its fishermen, because what he is asking is for us to give him carte blanche to do as he wishes. What would be more strengthening to the Canadian government in its negotiations with the United States-and we should reopen the question of interfering with their historic rights-would be to place it in a position to go to the international talks with other nations and say, "We have got the bill. We want to do it. It is just sitting back home waiting for us to come back and report the results of our negotiations." The government would be able to use that as the strongest possible lever to obtain the greatest possible benefits from the establishment of a 12 mile fishing zone.
If the government persists in demanding that this bill be passed in its present form, and continues to support that demand by the spurious reasoning that it will strengthen its hand in these negotiations which, incidentally, look so far as though they have been carried

out with an extremely weak hand, we can come to no other conclusion than that it is the desire of the government to give the least possible protection to the fishermen of Canada, and the greatest possible protection to the privileges of others who fish in our waters.

I think the government should be open and frank with members of this house before we endorse the principle of the bill. If the committee on marine and fisheries is to consider this measure, some specific answers will have to be given us with regard to the co-ordinates which will be setting up the base line, and we should be told in greater detail what is meant by respecting the traditional and treaty rights of fishermen from foreign countries, particularly the United States. If all the traditional rights and all the so-called treaty rights which United States fishermen claim can be exercised within the 12 mile zone and right up to the shores in Canadian waters, the establishment of a 12 mile zone would really be of no benefit to Canadian fishermen.
This is an important matter because, in effect, the bill before us amounts to an extension of the boundaries of Canada. Surely the government should give the house an assurance that it intends to make use of this measure to add some security to the rights of fishermen and the future of our fishing industry? I do want to bring to the minister's attention, as an old socialist and democrat, that the fishing companies in British Columbia-and, I presume, on the Atlantic coast to a similar extent-are either United States controlled or have very close connections with United States corporations and companies. As against that, the members of the unions involved are Canadian citizens who are trying to stand up for Canada's national rights. I think their representations with respect to the reference of this bill to the committee before second reading should receive greater consideration than the share capital invested in so-called Canadian companies by United States interests.
While this treaty points to fishing rights not to be allowed within the three mile limit, as I understand it, owing to the practice of using base lines from cape to cape in reality this treaty will permit fishing within the three mile limit at certain geographical points near the capes in question, and so on.
I want to deal briefly with the reference made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robi-chaud) to treaties. The Secretary of State for External Affairs speaks almost with awed breath when he deals with treaties of ancient history, and so on. I find on page 3660 of Hansard that the Minister of Fisheries had this to say:
On the Atlantic coast the United States has treaty rights in addition to claims of historic fishing, and for this reason alone is entitled to special consideration in any arrangements on fishing within areas that will become either internal waters or the contiguous fishing zone.
What is the history of the United States with regard to respecting treaties that have been signed on behalf of Canada? The government of the United States have not hesitated to violate any treaty whenever it was in their interest, and I can give the house proof of that right now. I became interested in this question when I was first elected to this house and began to study the Oregon treaty of 1846, which I was particularly interested in owing to the building of the Bonneville and Boulder dams on the Columbia river and the consequent impediment to navigation from the upper Columbia to the
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones sea, and the destruction of the heavy salmon run which came up into Canada when I was a boy. What happened on that occasion? We all know that the treaty was signed by the government of Great Britain and the government of the United States in 1846 and there were serious differences at that time as to the 49th parallel. It was decided finally, by mutual arrangement, that the government of Great Britain would secede all the land west of the Columbia south of the 49th parallel to the sea in return for the United States guaranteeing uninterrupted navigation to British subjects from the headwaters of the Columbia to the sea. I will deal with that point, Mr. Speaker, and refer to article II of the Oregon treaty which was signed on June 15, 1846, which reads in part as follows:
In navigating the said river or rivers-
That is the Columbia river:
-British subjects, with their goods and produce, shall be treated on the same footing as citizens of the United States; it being, however, always understood, that nothing in this article shall be construed as preventing, or intended to prevent, the government of the United States from making any regulations respecting the navigation of the said river or rivers, not inconsistent with the present treaty.
And then it goes on:
"From the point at which the 49th parallel of north latitude shall be found to intersect the great northern branch of the Columbia river, the navigation of the said branch shall be free and open to the Hudson's Bay Company, and to all British subjects trading with the same, to the point where the said branch meets the main stream of the Columbia, and thence down the said main stream to the ocean, with free access into and through the said river or rivers; it being understood, that all the usual portages along the line thus described, shall in like manner be free and open." That means that here is a solemn treaty in which the United States guarantees free access to the sea to British subjects in perpetuity.

Mr. Speaker, there are just one or two points I want to make on this bill. First of all I should like to say that I am no fisherman, nor do I come from the east or west coast, but there are things in this bill which I hope the committee will watch very closely.
I think that one of the predominant faults of this bill is that it is giving too much discretionary power to the minister and the government. I well remember in 1962 when hon. members opposite took four or five days telling those of us who were on the government side that we were giving too much power to the minister of national revenue in connection with a bill dealing with class or kind. We were told that the bill was wrong in principle. Now we have a bill before us giving altogether too much power to the minister and the government.
As I understand it, the minister can move these geographical co-ordinates at his own discretion at any time and at any point. We will find fishermen fishing inside the line drawn between two co-ordinating points in an area in which they should not be fishing,

and they will not know any different because an order in council had been passed. Perhaps this is one of the reasons the government has not been able to get the consent of other countries in the negotiations they have been carrying on. Why should this government present to the house a piece of legislation and ask the house to pass it before these negotiations have been concluded? I have never heard of anything so ridiculous or so silly since I came to this house. These negotiations should have been concluded before the legislation was introduced.
This is just another example of poor legislation which has been introduced to this house before enough homework has been done on it. We have had experience of this with the redistribution bill, the pensions bill, the flag and the 11 per cent building tax. We also had the suggestion for two ministers of agriculture put before us. All of these proposals have either been withdrawn or revised. Now the house is being presented with another such piece of legislation, and I am certainly glad it is going to the committee where it can be examined most carefully.
The government say that air lines should not worry about this legislation. International air lines cannot fly over territorial waters. We might find the minister or the government using these geographical co-ordinates as a bargaining weapon, a means by which they will make bargains with international air lines. Altogether too much power is being placed in the hands of one minister. The Conservatives have always believed in a 12 mile fishing limit, but we want to approach the matter in a right and proper way. The Conservative way is to negotiate first and then bring in legislation. But no; this government wants to put the cart before the horse and bring in legislation for approval before negotiations are complete. As I say, I am glad the matter is being put before the committee so that it can have a really close examination. A principle is involved here, namely the granting of too much power, and I suggest should not pass this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is appropriate, as far as I am concerned, that I should read the motion which is before us presently in order to be quite sure not to overstep the limits suggested to the house by the mover.
It reads as follows:

That an order of the house do issue for the production of all flag designs or models which have been received by the Prime Minister, members of the cabinet or the government, as models for a Canadian flag.

Now, the motion is for the production of what? Of all flag designs or models received by the Prime Minister, or the members of the government, as models for a Canadian flag. The first principle to be ascertained when we have a motion for the production of papers is whether or not such papers can be produced, in accordance with the rules of the house.
Now, I should quote from May's sixteenth edition, page 273, the following excerpt:

While the house has the power of ordering documents to be laid before it the papers sought should be of a public official character and not private or confidential.

The house is facing a very strange problem considering, first of all, the nature of the motion. The first thing to know is whether what is asked is the production of papers. If so, whether such papers are of a public, private or confidential nature.
In the first place, I asked for a report on the very nature of the designs submitted, and here is the answer given in this connection:

The 3,000 odd designs in the department of the Secretary of State are on various kinds of material including letter-paper, silk or cloth, heavy wrapping paper, canvas, hardboard, and plywood. In some cases actual flags were made up from bunting, nylon and other flag material. The designs range in size from a two inch by four inch pencil drawing to a five foot by three foot production in colour on hardboard.

It seems clear enough to me, Mr. Speaker, that many of these designs and models are not documents, but articles, as for instance a chair would be, and I suggest that the house has certainly no jurisdiction to order the production of articles which represent movables. I merely say that there is a serious question of whether or not those articles are papers, but this is neither the most important

part nor the most serious and definite argument against the motion.
The most important thing is first of all that the models and designs were, by nature, submitted in a confidential way, in the interest of ministers, for purpose of discusison in the cabinet, or for information and as suggestions to the Prime Minister himself.
But when I say that those documents are of a confidential nature, I contend that this appears in the act itself. Under not only the Copyright Act but also the international conventions governing this matter, it is clear that as soon as any design, model or work of art was not only conceived but transferred into a concrete shape, either as a design or an article, the person who conceived, draughted or created such a model has a copyright that nobody else can infringe.
In other words it is clear that if I, in the first place, were to create a work of art or make a design and if I submitted it as a suggestion, as long as I do not waive my copyright, as long as I do not grant permission to issue that design, I keep my copyright. It is not to be published. I am the only one entitled to decide whether or not the said design will be published or issued.
Therefore, if at least only the spirit of the law is applied to the things or the papers which the motion asks to be tabled, I say that those things which, because of their very nature, were submitted in a confidential way, as I said, only for the information of the minister or of the Prime Minister, because it is contrary to the law or to the nature of those things to publish or to reproduce them.
Second, if May's comment is applied to the principle I referred to a while ago, it is clear that such things cannot be the subject of a motion for papers, because the said papers would be confidential documents submitted for the information of the minister or the Prime Minister and not for publication or reproduction.
And that goes still further. Under the Crown Liability Act which, if I remember correctly, was passed by the federal parliament in 1952, the crown is henceforth subject to civic liability, the same liability for damages, as individuals. Now, if we decided or took the responsibility to publish or to reproduce the models or the designs for which each designer has a copyright, I say that we would infringe upon the copyright of each one of those who made the models or the designs and thus we would incur civic liability for the crown and we would be transgressing law.
Indeed the first right of an author is precisely that his work be not reproduced or

published without his consent, and the first transgression of that right is precisely the publication or the reproduction of the work without the consent of the author. I submit that it is surely not the purpose of the standing orders of this house or of any motion for papers to compel the crown or the government to incur a civic liability because of the breach of a statute.
That is another reason why I think we are not entitled to have printed and distributed hundreds of copies of the designs and projects which were submitted.
Moreover, what would be the use, for the purposes of the house as such-I would not say revelation-but of this reproduction? Would it be worthwhile to compel the government to break the law?
The government should take a decision as far as the design is concerned, from the designs submitted, and should choose one and recommend it to the house for adoption. Besides, the government is absolutely free to recommend some other design that has never been submitted.
Further, I would say that the motion under consideration at this time would not increase in any way the interest the house might have had in another motion that has already been tabled and which I shall not discuss, because it is not under consideration at present.
There is more; I must refer once again to the Copyright Act because it is essential, there is this: a model or design always remains the property of its author under the Copyright Act, unless the author himself agreed to the transfer of this property or of his copyright, or gave up his copyright in the work or design or in the model. Legally, the only consequence is that one and each of those designs and models remains the private property of the person who supplied it.
If we take for granted that it would still be documents, not only because the document is confidential, since it was submitted to the minister or the Prime Minister on a confidential basis, but it goes farther than that, we are simply and solely faced with articles which are the private property of those who submitted them for suggestion purposes. Now, it seems clear to me that the purpose of a motion for papers cannot be to obtain the production of what is the private property of a person. What can be obtained is the production of papers which are public documents.
I feel that if the confidence motion was to be eliminated, if desired, by saying: Well, if a flag has been submitted to a minister, it is because the minister is allowed to use it, nevertheless, the design or model remains

Once again, therefore, a motion for papers cannot be used to tell the government: well, those items, those things that were handed to the minister or the Prime Minister, we insist now, even if they do not belong to the minister or the Prime Minister or if they do not belong to the government, we insist now that they be shown to the house.
I think those are extremely serious reasons taken exclusively, but of necessity, from a federal statute enacted by this parliament and which this parliament ought to be the first to respect.

As fishermen they have always had a moving story to tell regarding their life on the sea, and the problems and dangers which surround them. Not the least of these dangers is the very grave one of not being able to find sufficient fish in the course of a season's fishing to meet the heavy expenses of operating expensive fishing vessels, and the expenses of competing in the coastal waters of Canada for their livelihood, not only against fellow Canadian fishermen but against fishermen of other countries encroaching closely upon the shores of Canada. This, basically, was the story they wanted to put to us and have us understand.
It is not a new story in itself, for again and again this very competent union has put its story, and put it ably, in talks which it has had with the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud). These union members have delivered briefs to each and every member of the House of Commons. They have visited on more than one occasion with members of the house to make them familiar with their case and their particular problems. They have a newspaper which is received regularly through the mail by members of parliament, a newspaper which keeps members in close touch with what they are doing and what they are thinking.
Therefore there was not anything new in what they had to say. They were bringing no new facts to light as they told us their story. They simply reiterated the very grave problems which they face. They told us it was their hope that their story would be told to the standing committee on marine and fisheries before second reading of the bill was reached. If this had been possible I am sure they would have told their story dramatically, and with all the emphasis which people, seeking their livelihood from fishing, can give to the expression of their problems. But I doubt that taking that story before the committee, and using the time of the committee to explain points that have already been made very clear, would have done much to improve upon the knowledge which the committee already has of the problem. Indeed, in doing so we might have run into some dangers.
It was made very clear by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), when he opened the discussion on the bill in this house on May 20, that negotiations and talks were already under way with other nations in regard to the effect of Canada's unilateral action in establishing the 12 mile limit, and that to open up these matters to

searching committee discussion, at a time when Canada was involved in delicate negotiations, would not be in the best interests of Canada.
Basically, what do these fishermen want? They would of course like to see all fishermen of other countries, even countries with historic fishing rights, excluded from Canadian waters and from within the 12 mile limit. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the problems attendant upon this will be clear to every member of the house. Such matters are those for most careful negotiation between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the secretary of state of the United States to establish how the problem of sharing the fisheries off the coasts of North America can best be handled.
An indication that this has been receiving the close attention of the government was given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he referred to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on his return from Hyannis Port when he said, as recorded at page 621 of Hansard for June 4, 1963, with respect to his discussions with President Kennedy:
I informed him that the Canadian government would shortly be taking decisions to establish a 12 mile Ashing zone. The President reserved the longstanding American position in support of the three mile limit. He also called attention to the "historic" and treaty fishing rights of the U.S.A., and I assured him that these rights would be taken into account. Discussions will be held with the United States with a view to determining the nature and extent of the U.S.A. rights and interests which may be affected by action which Canada is taking.
These negotiations are now in progress. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs said on May 20, as recorded at page 3411 of Hansard:
This is what the government of Canada is now in the process of doing. We have already had three rounds of negotiations with the United States. In the last two months we have had a round of discussions with Norway, Denmark, Britain, Portugal, Spain, Italy and Japan. All these countries sent officials to Ottawa to have talks with us, and in our negotiations with the United States one of the meetings took place in Washington. I am hopeful that in all cases our discussions will work out satisfactorily-
Now, Mr. Speaker, while these discussions of such a delicate nature are in process I think the house will understand that the best it could do at the moment in the interest of the fishermen would be to give second reading to this bill, and thus assure them that we have taken one more step towards recognition in principle of a 12 mile limit, on a unilateral basis, to protect the fishing industry of Canada, and that we intend to proceed with the next step from there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have no desire, and I certainly hope the impression is not left that we do have any desire, to disagree or quarrel with the decision the house has just made. We think it should have made a different decision, but it did not. We think it would have been the better course to follow if the house had made a different decision. However the bill is before us for second reading, and we are now in the position of saying that this is better than nothing at all.
We hope that when the bill gets to the committee this full, clear and deep examination which the Secretary of State for External

Affairs (Mr. Martin) has promised will take place, will in fact take place. I have noticed in the past that ministers of the crown have given the house similar assurances, but when the matter was referred to the committee the majority on the committee-this was when we used to have a majority on a committee- decided otherwise. So the assurances of the Secretary of State for External Affairs really do not mean anything because it is the committee which will decide what it will or will not discuss. However, it is good to have the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the record so that we can persistently point to it if any of the members of the committee try to stifle the examination or debate which will take place.
I should like to make a few remarks about what I think is an incorrect approach to the negotiations to which reference was made, and the course which those negotiations have followed. In the first instance the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) have each said that the basis for this bill is the brief which was presented by the Fisheries Council of Canada some time in January of 1963. I merely want to say that the fisheries council of Canada is not the only organization in this nation with an interest in the fisheries. In fact, it represents only one segment of the fishing industry, the employing section, and thus would likely take a biased and prejudiced approach. So I think it was wrong in principle to base the contents of the bill solely upon a brief presented to the government by one section of the fishing industry.
Second, I think it is wrong in principle to use the contents of that brief as a basis for negotiations. We have heard the cabinet say time and time again that they must not disclose what their position is, that they cannot make public what they are thinking about, that they want to approach the negotiations with the other nations with a strong hand and therefore they do not dare tell the parliament and people of Canada what they are doing. On the other hand, they claim they are basing their whole negotiations on a brief which is a public document. Thus, if that is the basis for their negotiations, they are in the position of only being able to retreat from that base and are not able to negotiate beyond the contents of that brief, because the pressures from other nations are directed toward making the Canadian government retrench and draw back from whatever position they may have started with, with respect to base lines, fishing zones or anything else.
Here are two things that are wrong: First, basing their approach upon the attitude of one segment of the fishing industry and, second,
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones saying that the attitude of that segment is the basis of negotiations, thus leaving the government in the position of only being able to
retreat, depending upon the amount of pressure exerted by other nations. They were wrong in principle in approaching these negotiations, because of the fact that from the very start they had given away two principal points. They gave away the opportunity to attempt to renegotiate the two existing treaties with regard to historic fishing rights claimed by the United States and France. It is a bad and terrible way to conduct negotiations to say to those with whom you are negotiating: We are going to give away some of our points before we even talk about these matters, so just discard this question of treaty rights and historic fishing rights and we will proceed backward from there. This is another opportunity afforded to other governments to force our government into retreating from what should be a firm and determined position.
Not only that, but in the course of this debate there came to light a most disturbing revelation. Let me quote from the opening remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on May 20. I do so in order not to fall into the possible error of misinterpreting what he said. At that time he said:
Canada has never published official charts showing the present base lines, but for at least parts of our coast the base lines follow the sinuosities of the shore.
In other words, the base line is measured from the high water mark. He went on to say:
Pending the establishment of straight base lines, the fishing zones will be measured from the existing ones. This is clearly provided for in the bill.
I take that to mean that from the present high water mark from which we now measure three miles we will measure 12 miles when the bill establishing the fishing zone comes into effect.

Following that we will then have secret negotiations, or by decision of the cabinet co-ordinates will be established and we will draw the base lines and measure the distance all over again. But with respect to the initially established fishing zone let me quote what the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) said on May 21. As everyone in the house knows, he is a prospective cabinet minister inasmuch as he is now in that esteemed position of parliamentary secretary, and presumably he speaks

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones with some authority. He pretty well reiterates what I have just said, but as found on page 3467 of Hansard he made this statement:
When this bill has been proclaimed Canada's fishing zone will extend nine miles beyond the present three mile limit. The function of this portion of the bill, as I understand it, is to establish the existence of Canadian fishing zones.
This is the important part.
Let me say here parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, that it is my understanding also that since these zones are shortly to be moved farther out to sea in many places-that is, just as soon as the straight base lines have been defined and published-these zones will not be enforced in their temporary locations.
What sort of admission is that for the parliamentary secretary to make when the parliament of Canada is being asked to enact a law to establish a 12 mile fishing zone, namely to say that this does not matter because we are not going to enforce it in any event? It makes an absolute ass out of the law that we are in the process of enacting. I think this is a disgraceful state of affairs, and another revelation to parliament and the Canadian people of the attitude of the government toward this vitally important question.
As has been mentioned a couple of times, before we even started discussions we gave away our position so far as these so-called historic and treaty fishing rights are concerned. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made this as clear as it is possible for him or anybody else to make anything clear before the banking and commerce committee, when he said it was never the intention of the government to interfere in any way with the existing treaties. On the 26th of May, as found on page 3620 of Hansard, the minister referred to the historic fishing rights, and I should like to quote from what he said. Incidentally he is a very quotable person. At times it is difficult to quote him with any clarity because he is so verbose and clutters his thoughts with so many words that it is difficult to distinguish just what is fact and what is fancy, but in this case he was particularly clear. He said:
There is no intention to interfere with the treaty or historic fishing rights of the United States, with whom the particular negotiation has been put in question by my hon. friend, and there is no justification for creating the suggestion that anything involving Canada's interest stands in jeopardy.
That is as clear as it is possible for anything to be clear. The Canadian government had no intention and does not intend to interfere with the historic fishing rights of the United States. This substantiates what I said earlier, that the government gave away one of the points of negotiation before even entering into negotiations. This was substantiated by the Minister of Fisheries on May


27 and I should like to quote from his remarks as found on page 3660 of Hansard. Incidentally, I should preface this by saying that he was referring to the thought that retaliation might be forthcoming from the United States if we took a firmer attitude on this question. He said:
Seeing that the interests of the United States fishermen in the areas affected by the establishment of a 12 mile fishing zone and straight base lines are being fully recognized, and I would hope my hon. friend agrees with me on this position, it is difficult to see how the question of retaliation by the United States should even arise.
I want to come back to this question of potential retaliation in a moment, but for the time being I want to stick to these two quotations. They represent a clear statement by the two responsible ministers that the so-called historic fishing rights to which they referred are fully protected now, fully recognized. They are given full protection in the future, perhaps forever, but this is not clear in the bill that is now before us.
We come now to the question of the reluctance or refusal of the cabinet ministers responsible to disclose to the house what are to be the co-ordinates from which or between which the base lines will be drawn. If as the two hon. gentlemen have said the historic fishing rights and treaty fishing rights of the United States of America are to be fully protected, then why do they not declare now what the base line and the co-ordinates will be for the west coast? The United States of America is the only nation in the world that has any treaty or historic fishing rights on the west coast. There are to be no negotiations, since these rights are fully recognized and fully established. What is wrong now with saying, since these negotiations are completed, here are the base lines? Then, at least parliament will be taken into the confidence of the two hon. gentlemen about this phase of it.
Perhaps they are going to make more concessions. This is a very incisive question. What sort of concessions are they going to make to the United States, to their friends south of the line? Why the refusal to disclose this information when it cannot possibly affect any negotiations because each of the ministers has said the position of the United States on the west coast will be fully recognized?
I can predict, I think, now what will happen. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robi-chaud) tried unsuccessfully yesterday to mislead the house into thinking that Dixon entrance, Hecate strait and Queen Charlotte sound would be enclosed within the lines. I will tell you what is likely to be the case. Obviously, because of the refusal to disclose at this time where the base line is going to

be drawn out there, the base line from headland to headland will be drawn in such a way that Hecate strait, Dixon entrance and Queen Charlotte sound will be left as international waters. Is there any reason why the minister cannot say now that the situation will be otherwise? We would certainly like to hear it. I think at this juncture, before the house is asked to pass this bill in principle, this is the sort of information that should be given to us.
Following their argument-I think it is an illogical one-but following their argument they may have a case for refusing to disclose this information so far as the east coast is concerned. They claim to be dealing with Denmark, Great Britain, Italy, Norway and other countries in connection with these so-called historic fishing rights. They may not want to disclose their hand at this stage, although I fail to see why. They disclose their hand to the United States and they give way on all points even before the negotiations take place.
This question is of vital importance to west coast fishermen, vitally important to the preservation and development of our fisheries out there. The refusal to disclose this information, unless there is a clear, adequate reason given for that refusal, would be tantamount to the admission that they intend to give more and more before the pressure of their very friendly neighbours, as they call them.
Before I sit down, I should like to make a reference to the thought expressed that there might be economic retaliation by the United States against our fishery exports to that country. I believe these exports total in the neighbourhood of $100 million per year in value. In the first place, I cannot see why there would be retaliation because each of the ministers has disclosed that the treaty rights and historic fishing rights of the United States are completely recognized. Why raise the question of potential retaliation?
In any event, let us look at a few statistics which I was able to obtain today from a United States publication of the department of interior, fish and wildlife service, bureau of commercial fisheries, entitled, "Fisheries of the United States for 1962." This publication came out in April of this year. Incidentally, these statistics are substantiated by our own statistics, but I thought that inasmuch as the United States are involved we should look at what they have to say on the question. The United States, from its own waters, cannot at this stage and have not been able for some years now, to catch sufficient fish for their own domestic consumption. There is some argument about this, depending upon whether you take into account their exports 20220-236i

There is some argument as to what this catch is in relation to consumption, but it ranges between one half and two thirds. No matter how you interpret the statistics, the United States cannot possibly obtain from its own waters more than two thirds of its domestic requirements. It must import at least one third which, in poundage value of edible fish products, is in the neighbourhood of 1.2 billion pounds and in non-edible fish products such as meals and oils, is in the neighbourhood of 75 million pounds, with a value of about $500 million.
For a number of years the United States has been in a position whereby they must import this amount of fish. One could say that if we get firm with them they may cut off importation of our fish and buy it from some other nation. But what sort of friends are they if they do that? We have been told by everybody from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) down, and from the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Martin) up, that they are the greatest bosom pals we have in the whole world; that the United States government are our friends and allies, and that they bestow love and affection upon us. What sort of friends are they if we as a small nation, one tenth the size in wealth and population, exert a little bit of national sovereignty for our self-preservation economically and for the preservation of our fisheries, and they turn around and wreak some economic retaliation against us? I just do not believe they would, or else the Prime Minister and his colleagues have been telling us a different story about this love and tenderness which exists between us and the United States.
I merely point out this one fact, if it is necessary, to show it clearly; and I do not know any other way to put it except to say in a rather blunt fashion that the government of Canada, in this as in other instances, obviously has not the intestinal fortitude necessary to protect fully the interests of the fisheries people in Canada.

Just in order to keep the record straight, Mr. Speaker, I think I should reply very briefly to the statement made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) to the effect that I have not kept my promise to the united fishermen and allied workers union that they would be given a chance to appear before the standing committee on marine and fisheries.
Just a few weeks after I assumed responsibility as Minister of Fisheries, on my first visit to the west coast, I met with representatives of the union and I made a definite commitment that the question of the north Pacific treaty would be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries before ratification or acceptance by the government. I had no way of knowing at that time that we would have three or four phases of negotiations. Later, I made a similar statement in the house.
