subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Postmaster General) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
AMENDMENT RESPECTING RENEWAL PROGRAMS, PUBLIC HOUSING PROJECTS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is my first comprehensive statement in this chamber as the minister responsible tor housing. If for no other reason, the social and economic implications to Canada of this very important subject would make it an occasion of great significance to me. It is also the government's first comprehensive statement with respect to housing.
The resolution is the forerunner of amendments to the National Housing Act which represent a basic change in our concept, perhaps I should say a completely fresh approach, to some of the most vexing housing problems facing the country.
The proposed amendments will introduce a new flexibility into our National Housing Act, both as to objectives and as to ways in which we should strive to attain these objectives. They will, I hope, influence for the better the lives of many thousands of Canadians, in cities and towns, both large and small in all parts of Canada. Here in the resolution, and of course, in the bill to follow, is the promise of new hope for lower income families, for elderly persons and for those who are forced to raise their children in slums or near slums. There is also an added measure of help for university students. Finally, there are broad changes designed to assist provinces and, through them, the municipalities, to meet some of their housing and other development needs.
In view of what I have said, the duty I am called upon to perform tonight carries with it a double satisfaction. It also carries with it an element of sorrow, since both the resolution and the amending bill represent years of thought, work and effort on the part of our former colleague in this house, the minister of national revenue at the time of his death, the late member for Nipissing.
The late Jack Garland was a member of this house for more than 14 years. During a large part of that time he was the opposition critic on housing matters. Throughout the whole of his adult life he had a vital interest in this subject and he acquired a vast knowledge of Canada's housing needs. Consequently, I am sure it did not surprise members of this house to learn that when he became a minister of the crown he was given

an opportunity to implement many of the policies and views that he had expressed when he sat on the opposition benches. The resolution now being considered and the bill to follow are largely Jack Garland's brainchild and I know I voice the sorrow and sincere regret of all hon. members that Jack Garland himself is not here to introduce this resolution and speak in support of it.
I should also like at this time to express appreciation of the work done on this particular resolution and on the bill to follow by another great Canadian, the late president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Dr. Stewart Bates, whose death earlier this week came as a shock to us all. As hon. members are no doubt aware, Dr. Bates served his adopted homeland, Canada, with brilliance and distinction both before and after he resigned as professor of commerce at Dalhousie University early in the war years to assume an important post in the federal Department of Fisheries. After three years with the fisheries department he became deputy director general of economic research in the department of reconstruction and supply, and one year later he became director general of that branch. In 1947, Dr. Bates was appointed deputy minister of fisheries. I could not help but think of him, as I listened to the debate which took place earlier this evening and this afternoon. He made a really great contribution to the department of fisheries, in working out a series of international fishery agreements, one of which was with the north Atlantic nations while the other-the Minister of Fisheries referred to it a few minutes ago-concerned the north Pacific.
Dr. Bates was appointed president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in December, 1954 and he held that office until his unexpected death on the evening of Sunday last. The late Dr. Bates worked closely with my predecessor, Mr. Garland, during the eleven months in which the latter was the responsible minister for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and he worked closely with me during the period which followed. I had hoped that Dr. Bates would be with me on the floor of the house, when the bill comes up for discussion. I know I voice the feelings of the sorrow and the sincere regret of all members of the house that he is not here to participate in these proceedings.
Looking back over the list of distinguished Canadians who preceded me as minister responsible for housing, I find that none of them was usually given to general statements about the basic questions of federal housing policy. Perhaps I have a less philosophical mind than most of my predecessors, but I

would find it extremely difficult to consider the details of the proposed legislation, without first giving some thought to the general state of housing in Canada and to the purposes which I, as a member of the government, believe we should be trying to achieve through our housing legislation.
Earlier this month I had the pleasure of participating in the opening ceremony of a federal-provincial housing project in the city of Saskatoon. While in that city I visited two other projects that were largely financed by the federal government, with a very substantial contribution from the Saskatchewan government. Since taking over as the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing, I have had occasion to visit many other housing projects in different parts of Canada, including Sarnia, Winnipeg, Vancouver and other cities, and I have been impressed by what I have seen in all these communities. But I have been even more impressed with the improvements that have taken place during the last 15 years in the design and construction of housing projects with which C.M.H.C. has been associated.
On June 26, the first federal-provincial housing project associated with urban renewal will be opened in the city of Winnipeg. It will be Winnipeg's very first urban renewal project. His Worship Mayor Juba has proposed that I encourage members of this house, who may find it possible to be in Winnipeg on June 26 to attend the opening ceremonies. The ceremonies will commence at eleven o'clock on the morning of Friday, June 26.
The federal government, the provincial government and the city of Winnipeg will be joint hosts on that occasion. The ceremony will be followed by a luncheon at the Fort Garry hotel, and members of this house and members of the other place, who may be in Winnipeg on that occasion are cordially invited to the ceremonies and to the luncheon at the Fort Garry hotel. If any hon. member can make it, if he will give his name to me, to my office or to my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet), we will see to it that the formal invitations to the ceremonies and to the luncheon are sent to all interested members.
Mr. Chairman, by any international standard Canadians generally are well housed. We have a population of approximately 19 million, housed in 4.8 million occupied housing units. Seven out of ten of these dwellings are relatively new, having been built since 1920. Only 5 or 6 per cent of these houses are described in the 1961 census as being in need of major repair. Ninety per cent of our Canadian families have the exclusive use of their own homes.
National Housing Act
Canada's population is increasing at the rate of about 400,000 persons per annum. This increase in population is accompanied, as all hon. members know, by a decline in farm population; thus the increase in other areas is such that as a nation we need an output of roughly 125,000 dwellings per annum in our cities and towns-not in the rural areas- merely to keep abreast of population growth in housing requirements.
Over the past ten years new housing and the repair and modernization of existing houses certainly has been sufficient to bring about a real improvement in the over-all housing situation in Canada. The number of doubled-up families has gone down by 150,000 during the period to which I have referred. Occupied dwellings in which you can get hot and cold running water has been increased during the same period by half a million. Between 1951 and 1961, there was a decline, I believe, of 400,000 or more in the number of occupied dwellings lacking modern toilet facilities. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, despite the generally high standard of housing conditions in Canada, and despite the recent and continuing improvement in the over-all situation, there are still far too many Canadians living in desperately inadequate and overcrowded housing units. Close to half a million families are still sharing accommodation with others, and one fifth of our dwellings in Canada still lack hot and cold water and modern bathing facilities. Fifteen per cent of our housing units or dwellings in Canada lack modern toilet facilities. The lack of amenities, as you might expect, is more pronounced in rural than in urban areas, but congestion in the cities, in the urban areas, is great, and even there the lack of amenities is shocking.
I think we can all get pleasure and satisfaction out of the very high-unusually high -average standard of housing in Canada, and we certainly can rejoice in the improvements to which I have referred. We can be gratified with the knowledge that assistance of one kind or another under our national housing acts has played a very considerable part in achieving our present standard and in improving it from year to year. But, Mr. Chairman, while we are in a mood of selfcongratulation let us not fail to accept some responsibility for the misery that persists in the slum and near-slum areas of at least some Canadian cities. Also let us not forget the danger that lurks in the fire traps, let us not forget the newspaper headlines that we see too often, particularly during the winter months, that tell of death by fire, by suffocation and neglect in many of our towns and cities.

National Housing Act
Alter nearly 20 years of steady improvement in average housing conditions in this country, is it not reasonable to ask one simple question? How long must the trend of improvement in average housing standards continue before we take steps, as a national parliament, to do away with some of the extreme privation that continues to plague large numbers of our fellow Canadians in their housing predicament? The answer to this question, to those who have visited Halifax, Saint John, Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, and Vancouver particularly-my home city-hits one in the face, and certainly there is no reason for any of us to be complacent or satisfied with what we find in these cities. We cannot go on indefinitely improving the average standard of housing conditions and not seriously try to do something worth while for the large numbers of people, who are forced to put up with accommodation that in some instances at least offends even the most rudimentary sense of human dignity.
Under the National Housing Act over the past ten years the production of half a million new houses has been subsidized or assisted in one way or another. Of these houses, 450,000-90 per cent-have been built under the insured loan provisions of the National Housing Act. That is to say 90 per cent of the entire housing output associated with the National Housing Act has been provided for the middle income or upper income classes. These are people who can afford new houses. But only 10 per cent of the N.H.A. output was provided under the sections of the act specifically designed to benefit people in the lower income brackets.
I submit it is clear from this pattern that Canadian housing policy has been heavily committed to the support and aid of the private market; and rather to the production of housing than to its distribution, which has been left almost entirely to these private market forces. I am sure that the government and all hon. members of this house fully support the good features of what has happened under our existing housing policy and favour its continuation. Perhaps one way to put it is to say that this continued improvement has become a basic fact of Canadian life. But while we may undertake to continue this policy, we must be careful not to give it our exclusive commitment, because there are many things which this type of public financing cannot do. For instance, it cannot assure us that we will be able to correct the worst housing conditions, housing conditions of the nature to which I referred a few moments ago. Admittedly correction of these conditions cannot be achieved either quickly or economically under what is

frequently called the "filtering down*' process. I think all hon. members know, what is meant by the filtering down process, and I believe we all subscribe to some degree of belief in that process. If you build houses for the middle or upper income class, the poor of course will benefit from some of the houses which are passed down to them by the upper classes. That will follow as daylight follows dark. The slum or near slum dwellers and the poor of this country-the residual legatees, if you want to put it that way, of this filtering down process-would be very much worse off, if there were no filtering down process. Nevertheless they do not get the type of help that I am sure members of this house want them to have. The filtering down process is too indirect. It is too uncertain; it is too slow; and it is too expensive in the long run.
In the view of the government, public housing offers a device by which additional housing can be made available directly at subsidized rents to those most in need, without requiring any diversion of the housing requirements of others. If the elimination of substandard housing conditions in Canada is among our housing objectives, as it should be, then we will have to depend largely upon public housing to achieve these objectives.
There has been provision for public housing in the National Housing Act for as far back as 1949. Section 36 of that act provided for the construction and operation of public housing projects by the federal and provincial governments on a 75-25 per cent cost sharing basis.
Some provinces, and more particularly Saskatchewan-I was very impressed by the developments I saw during my visit to Saskatchewan-have done more than others in this field. Projects are initiated by the municipalities with the approval of the provinces, and during the 15 years since this section has been introduced some 12,000 public housing units have been built in Canada. Of these only
9,000	have been let at subsidized rents geared to the tenants' income. The annual subsidy bill to the federal government for these houses for the people in the lower income brackets, and our elderly citizens, is $1.7 million, and in my opinion that is a shockingly low sum to pay for a country as rich as Canada.
There are well over 100,000 families in Canada, who are unable to go to the private market to obtain accommodation or to go on the market and get houses under the existing provisions of the National Housing Act. In the course of my visits during recent months, I have been taken to houses where the accommodation is shocking and would not be considered adequate under the most Spartan of

standards. In my view, and I speak as a minister of the crown, our best accomplishments in public housing are not impressive. In the view of the government it represents the greatest single area of failure in our federal housing policy.
As hon. members will see from the resolution, paragraphs (c), (d) and (e), the bill to be placed before them has as one of its principal aims a new emphasis on the needs of low income families. The bill itself will contain a new institutional framework for the provision of public housing.
As I mentioned earlier, the existing legislation does provide for federal-provincial partnerships engaged in public housing activities. Now it is proposed in this new resolution that the provinces, or perhaps I should say the municipalities which are designated by the provinces, may create and own public housing projects themselves. The federal government, through C.M.H.C., is to provide long term capital assistance in the form of loans and in the form of grants for such projects. If hon. members look at paragraph (c) of the resolution this becomes obvious. The federal government is also to pay a portion of the annual subsidies or operating losses of such projects created by the provinces or by the municipalities which they designate. That is also provided for in paragraph (c).
These projects, of course, will be reserved generally for the use of tenants unable to afford adequate accommodation on the private market. It will be largely up to the provinces and to the local government bodies designated by them to acquire and to build and manage these projects. The public housing contemplated-this is very significant-may consist of new dwellings or may consist of dwellings acquired or leased from the existing stock of units. As far as the government is concerned, non-self-contained as well as self-contained accommodation will be considered eligible under paragraph (d) of the resolution. The provision for provincial and municipal ownership to which I have just referred is considered fitting because of the wide range of responsibilities which must be assumed by the provinces, or rather by the designated municipalities. It seems obvious that the provinces will have to co-operate, and the success of the scheme to a large extent will depend on the co-operation we get from the provinces and the municipalities they designate. Even though this be so, it is not necessary for either provincial or local governments to choose this new course which is provided for in the resolution, because there is no change in what they have been able to do in the past. The existing legislation will continue.
While providing for the new techniques the legislation will not take away anything that
National Housing Act
is in the old section 36, and the arrangements for federal-provincial projects, financed on the 75-25 per cent basis, will remain. The purchase or lease of existing housing as well as the building of new houses will be possible under the new legislation. It is also significant that buildings that are not self-contained will be included in the new scheme.
In short, Mr. Chairman, the bill, which I hope we will be able to discuss in all its detail on a very early occasion, will, as the resolution indicates, offer a new technique for public housing. It will also provide for some amplification of present techniques. The goal of the legislation is frankly ambitious and it encompasses nothing less than a decent standard of housing for all Canadians.
I must point out, however, that, as I mentioned a moment ago, this objective cannot be secured by the federal government alone. It can be achieved only in those provinces which subscribe to and are prepared to share the purposes and aims of the new legislation and, of course, are prepared to share a portion of the costs.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the government has a flexible attitude toward the new legislation itself but not toward the objective. If within a reasonable time the legislation fails to produce the pace of activity that is needed to bring about our ultimate goal it will have to be reviewed. I believe, however, that as long as there is hard evidence of provincial dedication to the same goal as is outlined in the resolution, we will reach that goal together and we will reach it in our and not in somebody else's lifetime.
I turn now to another broad area of public policy toward which the proposed bill is directed. For the first time federal legislation is put forward which will encourage and assist municipalities, with appropriate provincial authorization and supervision, to conduct broad programs of urban renewal. Since the early 1940's-1944, I believe-the National Housing Act has offered aid to municipalities to acquire and clear worn out or substandard areas for urban redevelopment. The federal government has been willing to pay half the cost of buying and clearing blighted property, but there is a string attached to the existing legislation. It can only be done so long as there is housing before or after on the cleared site.
The federal government has also shared with the municipalities the proceeds from the disposal of cleared land. I remember one very shocking piece of land with which I am familiar, known as the Bluewater area in Sarnia. The development arose out of the exigencies of war, when there was a great deal of construction. Any kind of roof was

National Housing Act
good enough, and worse than a slum sprang up in a period of roughly ten years. These buildings have all been cleared out and removed, and under a bylaw of the city of Sarnia the property is being converted into a major new development area for industry. And so it should be because-

This area in Sarnia has been cleaned up and it is now being offered to industry. But there are other areas in many cities where it may be that the land should not be put to industrial purposes but should be residential. The provisions of the old act have encouraged five provincial governments and several municipalities to work along these lines. Altogether some 600 acres of urban land-and that is a lot of property- are either cleared or subject to a redevelopment program that involves slum clearance by bulldozer. Some $70 million has been or is being spent for the demolition of properties in these areas.
Municipal plans for redevelopment of cleared areas have led to the construction of a few public housing projects and the setting aside of land for parks and recreational purposes, all of which is commendable, as well as for commercial purposes. These redevelopment efforts reflect the concern of all three levels of government about the gradual spread of slums and blight and the ensuing depreciation that comes from slum areas and affects properties adjacent to slum areas.
I have spent a fair amount of time during the last two and a half months visiting some of these areas and considering reports that have come in to Central Montgage and Housing Corporation. I am firmly convinced that the course embarked upon by the late minister of national revenue when he put the N.H.A. resolution on the order paper during the first session of this parliament will commend itself to all members of the house. The plans included in the proposed new legislation call for the redevolpment of areas which would lead to the construction of public housing in some areas as well as commercial development in the same areas.
As I said before, these redevelopment efforts reflecting the concern of municipal governments can now be directed toward all these objectives. I say that for this reason. If studies are made of the data to which I have referred

earlier they will show that the average cost of clearing an acre of land in a municipality is roughly $100,000. That is the average cost; but in our two major cities, Montreal and Toronto, the average cost is $300,000 per acre. Under these circumstances it becomes necessary or advisable for the federal government to move in and assume a major share of the cost and, as is proposed by this legislation, lend money to municipalities or in some cases make funds available through grants to correct the situation.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman, or would you like me to continue and finish my statement tonight?

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last I directed the following question to the Minister of Labour:
Would he tell the house whether the figure for April 30, 1964, in today's answer to the written question of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) represents an increase or a decrease in unemployment in comparison with April 30, 1963?
The answer to the written question to which I have just referred gave the number of registered claimants for unemployment insurance at the end of each month from May 1963 to April, 1964. I suggest that to simply set forth the figures in this way does not provide information that is really useful or meaningful to the Canadian people. I feel it is an urgent national matter and that they deserve to have this type of information at this time in a way that really indicates the true situation with regard to unemployment in our country. I suggest that a simple comparison of figures, one month with another, within the same over-all 12 month period does not do this at all.
A simple comparison of this type, for example, does not take into account the seasonal factors. It ignores the fact that for certain types of jobs unemployment tends to rise in certain months of the year and therefore unemployment in Canada has had a certain tendency to rise in the months of winter and early spring. I believe that at this time the Canadian people are watching the operations of this government. They are continually forming judgments of its activities and results.
For example, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that they are most interested in the unemployment insurance fund. They note the deficit figures

CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES
subsubtopic: PROVIDING FOR EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter I wish to raise tonight arises out of the question I asked the Prime Minister concerning the plight of operators of small tourist establishments, marinas and marine installations on lake Huron, and especially on Georgian bay.
Georgian bay is particularly hit by the low water problem, for several reasons. First is the type of business that is operated on the bay and the limited season under which the operators have to work. There is also the fact that the prevailing winds in this area tend to aggravate the low water situation. These operators are really in a disaster area just as much as farmers with a crop failure or with a loss of markets, or workmen who are unemployed. Not only are these people in difficult circumstances themselves but they gain a large amount of tourist dollars for this country. They pay their regular income tax and in ordinary circumstances they ask for and receive no favours from the government. They are small businessmen who operate a business for a few short months of the year. They try to make a reasonable living for themselves and also they bring in tourist dollars which as we all know form a large part of the credit on exchange with other countries. These people are now in difficulty. They must stay in business both for their own livelihood and for the benefit of our tourist industry and national economy. If they go out of business and lose their customers it might be a long time before they recover.
The government has announced that aid will be provided. I am asking that the aid to be given be extended to small operators in present difficulties. Briefly, I am asking the government to include in the estimates which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has undertaken to introduce to the house soon a grant to these operators as a disaster grant on the following bases: first, that it be granted only for the purpose of dredging, dock extension or similar work to permit small commercial enterprises whose water access has been cutoff or reduced by low water to improve their ability to operate; second, that this grant be

limited to a prescribed figure in the area of $5,000 or $10,000, as a maximum. I have made a survey of a number of tourist operators in my area on Georgian bay and I believe $3,500 would be the average amount required to give these people the opportunity to recover from this disaster which has befallen them. Third, this grant could cover only out-of-pocket expenses. Fourth, it is suggested that the claims be submitted to the district marine agent or a prescribed official of the Department of Public Works who would inspect the location and verify the need for the work and the estimated cost.
This, in brief, is what I have asked. I asked the Prime Minister yesterday if any such arrangement was included in his proposal and he answered: I cannot answer that question now. I am given some measure of hope that perhaps the Prime Minister may have this in mind and I am raising the question particularly so that it will be brought in with the estimates which will be introduced. Since these estimates are being planned to meet the emergency I am hopeful that the government is meeting the request for a special spending estimate to take care of this particular situation. I know that public works are being provided for commercial navigation, but as to help for these people who are commercial operators in a small way, we are not sure. I want to draw this to the attention of the government to make sure that they are not overlooked.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschalelels (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES
subsubtopic: PROVIDING FOR EMERGENCY ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we all listened with interest to the observations made by the hon. member this evening.
The matter he raises is at considerable variance with the question he recently put to the Prime Minister.
The hon. member raises the case of the small tourist accommodation operators who, because of the low levels in the great lakes and Georgian bay will lose this year profits resulting from their normal operations in those areas.
I may tell the hon. member that within a few days-I do not know whether I will be in a position to do it on Monday, but surely at the beginning of next week-I shall make a statement concerning practically every aspect of what the Department of Public Works can do to offer a short term solution to those problems resulting from the low levels.
The dredging projects that the department is carrying out will undoubtedly be profitable to small operators of businesses located along navigable waters.
I wish to assure the hon. member that we will have a quite substantial sum of money in

the supplementary estimates to be brought forward shortly, precisely with a view to bringing a short term solution to those cases.
The most important thing for us-I think the hon. member will understand what I mean -is to begin by providing for ocean shipping, because we have along those rivers harbours which are the mainstay of those smaller cities. If we did not carry out dredging operations this year, those localities would become ghost towns.
That is why this matter is extremely important, something we are well aware of. We shall have, within a few days, substantial supplementary estimates.
What we shall do strictly for ocean shipping will also include those establishments and those tourist centres located along those rivers.
I hope that answers the question raised by my hon. friend.

subtopic: HOLDING OF UNITED STATES CITIZEN IN TORONTO JAIL
HOLDING OF UNITED STATES CITIZEN IN TORONTO JAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to discuss the case of Mr. Eric Hooper, not because I am concerned only with Mr. Hooper and what was obviously a tremendous injustice committed against him, but because I am concerned with the rights which all Canadians have believed were guaranteed to them and which this case demonstrates can be, and are being ignored very frequently by government departments, and particularly by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. It seems to me that the rights which we have always thought were guaranteed to us are as follows: First, the right of a person accused of a crime to be charged within a very short period of time after he has been detained; second, the right of a person to have counsel; third, the right of a person charged not to be intimidated by the government officials questioning him; and fourth, the right of a person accused to be arraigned before a judge or a magistrate within 24 hours.
Mr. Hooper was arrested on February 16, apparently because it was charged that he had assaulted his estranged wife. That charge was dropped in a fairly short period of time; but instead of being released from the Don jail he was held for 96 more days until he was brought before a magistrate. Then when he was brought before the magistrate he was charged with a very serious offence, and I quote from the charge:
-you unlawfully refused to answer a question put to you. under section 50 of the Canada Immigration Act.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
But, Mr. Speaker, the questions he refused to answer were asked of him on March 23. Why was this man held in the Don jail from February 16 to March 23 when the hearing was held? I think one of these days-

speechtext:
-the minister is going to have to face up to the problem of these people in difficulties with the immigration department being held in places like Don jail, Bordeaux jail and others which I hope the minister will tell us about at an early time.
After the hearing was held it took them another nine weeks before his case was brought to court. I should like the minister to tell the house and the people of Canada how much longer it would have taken had not this man finally got word to a lawyer that he was being held for this length of time. If the Toronto newspapers had not carried this case as a front page story, would this man have been held another 96 days or 196 days? This is a very important question. I wonder whether the immigration officials or the minister think for one moment that Mr. Hooper would have stayed in jail for nine days, let alone 96 days, had he had the money to get a lawyer. I wonder whether Mr. Hooper would have stayed in jail for this period of time had his colour been white instead of black. It seems to me that here is another case of one law for the rich and another for the poor.
At the immigration department board of inquiry held in the Don jail, Mr. Hooper claims he refused to answer questions until he got a lawyer. The Minister of Justice denied that today but I think this claim is worth looking into. Mr. Hooper claims that one of the immigration officials at this hearing told him-and I am quoting from Mr. Hooper's words as reported in a Toronto newspaper-"You'll rot here till you're ready to talk". I suggest that Mr. Hooper should have been kept in Canada long enough to find out whether the words he alleged were used were in fact true. Because if they were, the official who used those words should have been fired immediately. Instead, the department then got busy and got him out of the country so that we could not get the real facts. There is no other reason for moving quickly at the time they did.
Mr. Hooper rotted in the Don jail for 57 days until a charge was laid on May 19. Then he appeared in court a week later only to be sent back to jail because the case was remanded. Why was the case remanded? Because after all this period of time the department did not hire a lawyer to represent them until the day the case came to

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion court; and of course the lawyer needed time to study the case. Surely the department could have hired a lawyer a little earlier, and surely they could have hired a lawyer who was not so busy that he did not have time to look into the case properly. But obviously the department were not worried about Mr. Hooper. I think that some of the departmental officials should be sent to jail for a week to see how they feel about it; and after that they might have a heart, which they do not seem to have now.
The case was to be heard on a Monday. On the Monday the magistrate freed the prisoner on his own recognizance. The department then acted quickly. Mr. Hooper was seized, taken back to jail and deported. After all those weeks why not let Mr. Hooper stay in Canada until the facts could come out? What was the department afraid of, and for whom were they covering up? How many other people are there locked up? The lawyer who acted for Mr. Hooper is quoted in both of this evening's Ottawa newspapers as saying that he understands there are ten other people held on the instructions of the immigration department in the Don jail who have been there for more than a month.

subtopic: HOLDING OF UNITED STATES CITIZEN IN TORONTO JAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to clarify some facts stated by the hon. member, regarding the number of people detained in our Canadian jails under the Immigration Act.
According to information obtained today from the department, only 16 people at the present time are being detained in Canada for deportation purposes, under the Immigration Act. Out of those 16 people-
One hon. Member: For how long?

subtopic: HOLDING OF UNITED STATES CITIZEN IN TORONTO JAIL
speechtext: -six have been detained for more than 30 days.

subtopic: HOLDING OF UNITED STATES CITIZEN IN TORONTO JAIL
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: HOLDING OF UNITED STATES CITIZEN IN TORONTO JAIL
speechtext:
There are two main reasons why those six people are being detained: they may have taken legal proceedings to have the order of deportation issued against them quashed and their right to stay in Canada recognized or arrangements may be under way
with the various countries concerned to secure their authorization for the deportation of some of those people to the countries where they are to go.
That is a first correction. Now, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) has given all the facts relating to the case and it stands out that the proceedings which were first taken before the Ontario courts took some time. The officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration came into the picture only when it was decided to withdraw the charge laid against Mr. Hooper.
The longest period runs between March 23 and May 5. What happened during that time? An investigation was made. Mr. Hooper was called and refused to answer. The investigation was postponed for a few days; he was called again and again he refused to answer. Then it was pointed out that Mr. Hooper was married to a Canadian woman and that he had a child here. The case thus became very important and was referred to the department for consideration. The department needs three weeks to study thoroughly the case of a person who has someone in Canada, a wife and a child were involved in this case. The investigation continued and in view of what came to light, the department decided that proceedings were justified. On May 5, at the department's request, proceedings were instituted against Mr. Hooper.
It is from that time that two appearances are made before the courts. Adjournments are requested, as is done in many cases.
I would state, therefore, that Mr. Hooper was held prisoner under Canadian laws and enjoyed all the privileges granted to a Canadian resident, even though he is not a Canadian citizen, but an American citizen. Therefore, in the case of Mr. Hooper, there has not been any undue delay, but in the future proceedings initiated by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will always be as expeditious as possible, and we shall always show the greatest respect for those who reside in Canada, even illegally, and even for those who must be deported for having violated our laws.

Ninety six days in jail without a lawyer. Liberal freedom.
